name: North Chute

ways.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, then up Avalanche Canyon past the South Chute
ways.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow in the chute is an improvement on the scree, but Avalanche Canyon is named for what runs down it in May and June
ways.notes:
Bike or walk the closed Dosewallips Road (FS 2610) about 5 miles to the Lake Constance climbers' trail, then the steep, unmaintained trail roughly 3,300 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camp at the north end of the lake.

From the lake, head north into Avalanche Canyon. This route is the parallel couloir further into the canyon: where the standard South Chute line turns east and climbs out early, the North Chute keeps you in the canyon bed longer and climbs from higher up it.

It sees less traffic than the South Chute and is commonly used as one half of a loop — up one, down the other — rather than as a route in its own right. It rejoins the standard line where the South Chute's gully tops out, crosses the Finger Traverse (or the Terrible Traverse when conditions allow), and finishes over the summit block and the North Chimney.

ways.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes: The alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail. Road-walk or bike roughly 6.5 miles from the washout past the Lake Constance turn-off to the road end at the old campground and ranger station, then the Constance Pass Trail south and southwest to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin, and climb to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass drop south into upper Avalanche Canyon. This is the variant that suits this route best of the three Constance routes, because the North Chute is the higher of the two chutes and coming in from Crystal Pass you meet it without walking the whole canyon up from the lake.

priorPrimaryResearch: Paragraph is the Lake Constance trail into Avalanche Canyon (v0), the standard Constance approach; v1 Crystal Pass is the long alternative.

name: Lynch Glacier

ways.name: Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond, then the east ridge and Lynch draw
ways.season: Jun-mid Jul, while Pea Soup Lake is frozen and the moat closed; the lake crossing gets hard once it melts
ways.notes:
Hike the Cathedral Rock Trail to Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) at 2.5 miles, continue to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, then turn left (west) onto the PCT. In less than half a mile turn right (northwest) onto Trail #1375 — do not follow the PCT down toward Deep Lake. Follow #1375 past Cathedral Rock to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft and camp there. This is the shorter approach with the longer summit day, and it avoids the brush of the alternative.

From camp, climb to about 6,300 ft on the east ridge, then traverse below the Daniel Glacier at 6,100 to 6,300 ft toward Lynch draw.

Trailhead to camp is about 2.5 to 4 hours; camp to summit 5 to 7 hours.

ways.name: Deception Pass, Marmot and Jade Lakes, and Dip Top Gap from the east
ways.season: Early season, roughly June into July, before the moat opens
ways.notes:
From the Deception Pass trailhead, hike to Marmot and Jade Lakes and continue to Dip Top Gap. From the gap, traverse west to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage, then descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.

This is the longer, eastern line into the same basin. It reaches the Lynch Glacier at the same point the Peggy's Pond approach does, and everything about identifying the ice is identical from the lake outlet onward.

priorPrimaryResearch: Mountaineers Lynch Glacier route uses Cathedral Rock TH -> Cathedral Pass -> Peggy's Pond; variant 1 notes itself call Deception Pass/Dip Top Gap 'the longer, eastern line'. Prose paragraph describes the Deception Pass line. (Variant 0's season text reads like the Pea Soup approach's and may be misfiled.)

name: Standard Trail (Upper Trailhead, NFR 24)

ways.name: Upper Trailhead on NFR 24, Trail #812 summer route
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Oct for the snow-free summer trail; outside that the chute fills and the upper switchbacks are buried
ways.notes:
From the Upper Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24 / FS 2419 — vault toilet, picnic table, Northwest Forest Pass required — Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is stacked stairstep switchbacks through forest, merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft.

From the merge, continue up the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline at about 4,500 ft, roughly a mile in. In summer conditions the trail is snow-free and well cut essentially to the top, switchbacking across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes to the 5,944 ft summit. Total gain from the Upper Trailhead is 2,444 ft over 1.6 miles one way. No water on the upper route; carry all you need.

ways.name: Lower Trailhead, the long approach to the same trail
ways.season: Roughly Jun-Oct, and it is snow-free earlier than the upper road in some years
ways.notes:
The Lower Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft, 3.1 miles one way, and takes no fee. It welcomes you with an easy grade rather than the upper trailhead's near-immediate jolt, and it is the sensible choice when FS Road 2419-014 to the upper lot is snowed in or gated.

It climbs steadily through forest and joins the upper-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. Everything above the merge is identical.

ways.name: The winter chute, direct from the timberline junction
ways.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, while the chute holds a firm continuous snowpack
ways.notes:
Not a different trailhead but a genuinely different climb, and it is what most parties are on outside core summer because the summer switchbacks are buried. From either trailhead, follow Trail #812 to the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and take the right-hand branch straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute below the summit saddle.

This demands an ice axe and traction — crampons or microspikes — and it is steep, funnel-shaped slide-path terrain with real avalanche potential. Check avalanche conditions before going up.

It is also the fast descent when conditions allow: with an axe carried in self-arrest position, parties glissade roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes. That is consequential terrain rather than a casual slide.

priorPrimaryResearch: Route is named for the Upper Trailhead; variant 1 is the lower TH fallback and variant 2 the off-season chute. Prose describes the upper TH summer trail.

ways.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing runs through avalanche terrain earlier than that
ways.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. It exists because the alternative is the ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin, which gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly. A third option starts at Cottonwood on the Entiat River and reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier. All three converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must drop about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.

ways.name: Holden Village and Copper Basin
ways.notes: From Holden Village up to the Copper–Entiat divide and the east ridge. The most direct way to the standard east-side line, and climbable in a day from Holden, but it depends on the Lake Chelan boat.

ways.name: Entiat River from Cottonwood
ways.notes: Up the Entiat River trail toward the Entiat Glacier and the east ridge. The longest way in, with less gain and little avalanche exposure.

name: Standard Scramble (Constance Pass / Home Lake)

ways.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake and Constance Pass
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Oct per NPS guidance for the Constance Pass and Home Lake corridor; earlier trips should expect lingering snow
ways.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,880 ft at the end of FR 2870, follow Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 south along the Dungeness River. The first mile is mostly flat; stay left at the Royal Basin Trail junction near a mile. Camp Handy — riverside meadow with a cedar shingle shelter — comes at about 3.4 miles.

Just past Camp Handy the trail forks; take the uphill fork and begin a sustained, largely switchback-free climb of about 3 miles and 1,800 ft to Boulder Shelter at 6.4 miles and about 4,890 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the whole approach — treat it as the last sure fill-up. Bear right at the shelter onto the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail. The park boundary is about a mile beyond, after which brush closes in from both sides.

The final 2.9 miles to Home Lake at 5,330 ft, roughly 9.3-9.6 miles from the trailhead, climb another 700-900 ft through subalpine forest into heather meadows, crossing two or three small streams; one waterfall crossing is awkward to keep feet dry and is slick with a full pack early season. Home Lake is the standard basecamp for Fricaba, Hal Foss, Mystery and Deception.

From camp continue on climbers' paths — no maintained tread — up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, then traverse and descend west into upper Deception Basin.

ways.name: Royal Basin and the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The other way into the same basin, and the one that suits a party doing Fricaba alongside Mystery and Deception. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead take Trail #833.2 about a mile and bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail #832 at the fork just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the basecamp; upper Royal Basin camps sit around 5,800-6,200 ft.

From upper Royal Basin climb the moraine and a 35-40 degree snowfield to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend scree to the grass and heather benches above Deception Basin. Fricaba is then across the basin to the east.

One published day-2 description of this side has parties angling up toward the pass going east for Fricaba, then round to the left of some gendarmes and up a steep scree route the account calls self-explanatory.

priorPrimaryResearch: Paragraph describes Upper Dungeness to Home Lake and Constance Pass (v0), named in the route title; Royal Basin is the alternative for multi-peak parties.

name: Southeast Slope via Methow Pass

ways.name: Rainy Pass, the crest trail to Methow Pass, and the east ridge
ways.season: Late June through September, with July through September giving the driest scree. June ascents work but the final slopes and gully still hold snow and want an axe and crampons. The highway is shut for avalanche control through the winter, which closes both approaches outright.
ways.notes: The long way, and the one that suits a two-day trip. From the large paved lot on the north side of SR-20 at Rainy Pass, follow the crest trail north as it climbs steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland past Porcupine Creek — fill up there, it is the last easy water before a long dry stretch of switchbacks — to Cutthroat Pass. From the pass the trail drops toward Granite Pass and a saddle beyond it, where a steep snowfield often lasts into August and has caused slide-for-life falls, so carry an axe if you are early in the season. Beyond, the trail contours across open, sparsely treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow, a common water and camp stop, with a short side trail west into the Snowy Lakes basin for a higher and more scenic bivy under Tower Mountain and Golden Horn. From the meadow, stay on the crest trail north to the open plateau at Methow Pass and leave it there: travel west and southwest off-trail through open heather and talus benches toward the peak's east ridge, gain the ridge, and follow moderate sand, scree and talus — loose in places, with real route-finding — up to the saddle between the true summit and its lower false summit.

ways.name: Swamp Creek pullout and the south ridge
ways.season: Late June through September once the snow finger has stabilised or melted, with July and August driest. Earlier in the season the finger is a snow climb rather than a scramble.
ways.notes: The short, steep alternative, and the way most day parties go. Start from the highway pullout at Swamp Creek and climb through brushy forest to the foot of the prominent ridge on the mountain's south side. Follow the ridge upward, staying on the crest where it lets you and moving climber's right to get around the cliff bands that block the crest around 5,200 ft — getting that traverse wrong is what turns parties back. Above the cliff bands the ridge opens out onto sand and scree and continues to the summit block. This side faces the sun and dries early, which is why it comes into condition before the crest-trail approach and why it turns into a loose, dusty grind by late summer; a snow finger on this flank can hold firm snow at a fairly steep angle into early summer, which speeds the ascent considerably for a party carrying an axe.

priorPrimaryResearch: The Mountaineers' standard Hardy route is the South Face from the Swamp Creek pullout (4.5 mi/4,100 ft), and variant 1's own notes say most day parties go that way; the prose describes the long PCT/Methow Pass line. Medium because the route name (SW Slopes snow/scramble) could also fit a multi-day trip from Rainy Pass.

ways.name: First Divide from the Duckabush and Marmot Lake
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: The historic Skokomish approach is closed by fire damage, and so is this one where it leaves the Duckabush: the park lists the Home Sweet Home Trail, from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide, closed for the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire with no reopening date (trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. When it reopens, the way in is the long Duckabush valley over Big Hump to Marmot Lake, then back to the Home Sweet Home junction and over First Divide. Roughly double the old distance and firmly a multi-day trip with a camp at the lake or at Home Sweet Home.

ways.name: Staircase and the North Fork Skokomish to First Divide
ways.notes: The historic and shortest way in. From Staircase, follow the North Fork Skokomish trail up the valley to Home Sweet Home and on to First Divide, where the scramble leaves the trail. Fire damage has affected this corridor, so check the park's trail status before planning.

name: South Slope

ways.name: Merritt Lake Trailhead and Nason Ridge Trail to Crescent Lake
ways.season: July into October once the ridge clears; snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring.
ways.notes: The shorter and more direct way in. From the highway turn onto the rough forest road — high clearance is worth having — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Climb the Merritt Lake trail to the lake, then join the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it east to Crescent Lake, which sits below the peak's south side. Water is available at Crescent Lake but is unreliable higher on the mountain, so fill there. The trail is well defined the whole way to the lake, and everything above it is your own route-finding.

ways.name: Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock–Crescent col
ways.season: July into October. Snow lingers above about 5,000 ft into late spring and the col holds it longest.
ways.notes: The longer and more scenic way in, and the one commonly used by parties who want the neighbouring summit in the same outing. From the highway near the milepost, climb the Rock Mountain trail to Rock Lake — snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring on this side — then cross the col between the two peaks and descend roughly five hundred feet on the far side to Crescent Lake. From there the climb is the same as from the other trailhead. It costs a substantial descent that has to be regained on the return, which is the price of the extra ground it covers.

priorPrimaryResearch: Merritt Lake is described as the shorter, more direct way in. Rock Mountain is used mainly by parties combining two summits. The paragraph describes both trailheads.

ways.name: From Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Lago is the highest peak in this group and the least loved underfoot, being a large pile of loose rock where the whole ascent asks for deliberate movement rather than any technique. Camp is normally Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin, reached along the Middle Fork Pasayten, either over Robinson Pass from the low Robinson Creek trailhead or down the Whistler Cutoff from the high start at Slate Pass, with an awkward crossing of upper Eureka Creek when it is swollen with snowmelt. From camp the round trip is a half day. Many parties link straight over to Carru by the connecting col rather than descending and re-climbing, and the southwest slope is a common variation for coming down since it avoids some of the steeper upper rock ribs.

ways.name: From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten
ways.notes: The high start most parties use. From Slate Pass the trail drops north into the Middle Fork Pasayten; follow it down-valley past the Berk Creek junction, then climb to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin to camp. Lago is usually combined with Carru and Osceola.

ways.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
ways.season: July and August
ways.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail south for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass. A southern alternative reaches the same pass from Stehekin: the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp — with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the Fremont Glacier saddle around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.

ways.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail to Park Creek Pass
ways.notes: From the Park Creek Trailhead on the Stehekin Valley Road, the Park Creek trail climbs to Park Creek Pass and joins the Thunder Creek line there. It needs the Lake Chelan boat and the Stehekin shuttle to reach the trailhead.

ways.name: Easy Pass and Fisher Basin
ways.season: July to September; the Easy Pass trail usually holds snow until July
ways.notes:
The usual way in while SR 20 is open. From the Easy Pass Trailhead near milepost 151, climb about 3.5 miles to the 6,500-ft pass, drop into Fisher Basin, and follow the Fisher Creek Trail down the valley — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. About ten miles one way. The trailhead sits inside the highway's winter closure, and the pass is often snowbound until July.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.

ways.name: Thunder Creek and Fisher Creek
ways.season: Whenever SR 20 is closed at Easy Pass, or in the shoulder season
ways.notes:
The longer way in, and the one that stays open all year: the Colonial Creek trailhead is west of SR 20's winter closure gates. Take the Thunder Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground near 1,200 ft about nine miles to the Fisher Creek Trail junction, then the Fisher Creek Trail about three miles, past the handrailed log bridge, to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft. Roughly thirteen miles one way, with Neve Camp under two miles in for a late start.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.

name: North Face

ways.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col
ways.season: Best while the face still holds continuous snow and ice, roughly Jun into mid-Jul; it used to hold year round and no longer does
ways.notes: Drive the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, roughly twenty-two miles and turn right onto the Phelps Creek road, FR 6211, to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow. Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. It is sometimes called the Carne Mountain High Route, but the two are also treated as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable. It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Good camping and water. Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. Keep climbing cross-country over meadow, scrub, talus and probably snow to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col at about 8,150 ft, north-west of Maude's summit.

ways.name: Entiat River and Ice Lakes from the east — the first-ascent line
ways.season: Same window; this side is a much longer walk and is mostly used by parties already camped at Ice Lakes or exiting that way
ways.notes:
Drive the Entiat River Road and walk the Entiat River trail #1400 about eight and a quarter miles to the Ice Creek trail. The Entiat River has to be crossed on logs, and if there is no log at the trail there may be a large jam south of it.

The first-ascent party did not follow the river to the meadows at its head. They walked instead to the col between Spectacle Buttes and Maude's south-east side and dropped from Ice Lakes onto the slopes beside the face, judging it more direct and free of bushwhacking. That cost them nearly three thousand feet of climbing to reach Ice Lakes.

priorPrimaryResearch: Variant 1's own notes say the Entiat side is much longer and used mainly by parties already at Ice Lakes. Phelps Creek to Leroy Basin is the standard way to the north face. The paragraph describes both.
